paras: The attempted lynching of two tramps at Rock Springs was a mob hanging in Wyoming Territory, reported in July 1888, in which residents strung up two unnamed men suspected of a robbery. Both men protested their innocence and were let down alive just before death, after which they left town. Wyoming papers repeated the story in brief as a warning to tramps.

According to the Rock Springs Independent, which gave what one paper called an "extended account," two tramps "supposed to have committed a robbery" were taken out by "the populace" and strung up. Neither the men nor the robbery's victim was named, and no date was given beyond the Platte Valley Lyre's word that it happened "recently." Both men protested their innocence and were let down "just before death intervened." The Lyre added that the two, described as "accused of robbery," were "half strangled" and then left town.
No report of an arrest, inquest or prosecution of anyone involved appears in the coverage.

The episode appears only in short exchange paragraphs in Wyoming papers; the Independent's original account does not appear in the coverage. A territorial round-up column of July 17 summarized it and closed with the remark that "Rock Springs is a very good town for tramps to stay away from." Bill Barlow's Budget of Douglas reprinted that paragraph almost word for word on July 25.

The Platte Valley Lyre of Saratoga wrote its own version on July 19, saying Rock Springs had adopted a rope with a noose as a "tramp remedy" and calling the men "ragged rascals." It ended with "A second dose was not needed," treating the hanging as an effective way to drive the men out. None of the papers questioned the mob's action or mentioned the men's race.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of two tramps at Rock Springs
bases: A crowd described as 'the populace' strung up two men suspected of robbery and let them down alive before death, an attempted lynching by hanging (A1, A2).

The two men were hanged by 'the populace' on suspicion of robbery but were let down 'just before death intervened' and later left town, so no one was killed and the episode falls short of a completed lynching (A1, A2).

All three items are brief exchange paragraphs that appear to derive from one account, the Rock Springs Independent's, which A1 names as its source and A3 reprints word for word; A2 is worded differently but adds no independent sourcing (A1, A2, A3).
